title: 3. Principal component analysis
text: This script runs a principal component analysis (PCA) of the seven log antibody levels, then asks whether the principal components predict cryptococcosis status. The correlation plots and PCA plots are drawn in Figures, and the eigenvalue table in Tables.

title: 3. Principal component analysis
text:
Why PCA
The antibody levels are correlated with one another, most strongly GXM-IgM with Lam-IgM (see the correlation plots in Figures), which makes their individual coefficients in a joint regression model unstable. PCA was used to account for this correlation (Yoon et al. 2022): it re-expresses the seven measurements as seven uncorrelated components. The first component, PC1, acts as a summary score of overall antibody level. It runs opposite to the antibodies, so a higher PC1 means lower antibody levels.

title: 3. Principal component analysis
text:
Fit the PCA
PCA is run on the log antibody levels of participants with complete antibody data. scale = TRUE standardizes each antibody first, so that no single antibody dominates because of its units.


Click to show/hide R Code
#PCA analysis

#Run PCA on log of titer data
PCA<-CleanData_NoMissingTiters%>%
  select(LogTiterVariables)%>%
  prcomp(scale=TRUE)

title: 3. Principal component analysis
text:
Component scores
Each participant’s scores on the seven components are added to the data. Figures includes a correlation plot confirming that the components are uncorrelated.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Add PCA results to CleanData_NoMissingTiters
columns<-predict(PCA)
PCAData<-cbind(CleanData_NoMissingTiters, columns)

title: 3. Principal component analysis
text:
Do the components predict cryptococcosis?
A logistic regression of cryptococcosis status on all seven components. Because all seven are included, the model as a whole fits exactly as well as one using the seven log antibodies directly; the difference is that each component’s coefficient can be read separately. The question of interest is whether the summary score, PC1, is associated with case status.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Are the principal components predictors of cryptococcus status?
pc_regression_table <- glm(HasCryptococcus ~ PC1+PC2+PC3+PC4+PC5+PC6+PC7, family = binomial, data=PCAData) %>%
  tbl_regression(., exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()

title: Clinical background
text:
Among invasive fungal infections in organ transplant recipients, cryptococcosis ranks third in frequency (Baddley et al. 2019), and it carries substantial mortality (Yoon et al. 2022).
Two kinds of antibody are relevant to Cryptococcus neoformans:
Both have been linked to cryptococcosis, or to the risk of developing it, in people with HIV (Subramaniam et al. 2005; Hlupeni et al. 2018; Yoon et al. 2019) and without HIV (Rohatgi et al. 2017). In transplant recipients, Jalali et al. found pretransplant GXM-IgM lower, but posttransplant GXM-IgM and IgG higher, in patients who developed cryptococcosis (Jalali et al. 2006). This study measured both antibodies, together with total (non-specific) IgM, IgG1 and IgG2, in transplant recipients with and without a history of posttransplant cryptococcosis (Yoon et al. 2022).

title: Clinical background
text:
Study design in brief

Setting: University of Alabama at Birmingham; recruitment 1 January 2013 to 31 December 2018.
Cases: organ transplant recipients with a history of posttransplant cryptococcosis, diagnosed from a positive cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) result or a positive body-fluid culture.
Controls: organ transplant recipients with no such history.
Measurements: serum total IgM, IgG1 and IgG2 (µg/mL, Luminex); GXM- and Lam-binding IgM and IgG (titers); serum CrAg by lateral flow assay.
Approvals: the UAB Institutional Review Board approved the study and all participants gave written informed consent; the samples were analyzed at Albert Einstein College of Medicine under a protocol approved by its IRB.

See analysis-plan.md for the full specification.

text: This script attaches every package the analysis uses and says where to find the study workbook.

title: Setup
text:
Packages
The package list is the one used for the published analysis:

Data import and management: readxl reads the Excel workbook; tidyverse (including stringr) handles cleaning and reshaping (Wickham et al. 2019); haven supplies as_factor(), used to turn categorical variables into factors.
Tables: gtsummary builds Table 1 and the regression tables (Sjoberg et al. 2021); bstfun adds the inline forest plots to those tables; flextable formats the PCA eigenvalue table.
Figures: ggplot2, ggbeeswarm (quasirandom points) and ggpubr (Wilcoxon p-values on the plot); corrplot for correlation matrices.
Modeling: broom (attached, but not called directly by the scripts); pROC for ROC curves and AUC confidence intervals (Robin et al. 2011); cutpointr for optimal titer cutpoints (Thiele and Hirschfeld 2021); factoextra for PCA eigenvalues and plots.

bstfun is not on CRAN; install it from GitHub with remotes::install_github("MSKCC-Epi-Bio/bstfun").

Continuous variables were compared with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and categorical variables with Fisher’s exact or χ² tests. Median age was 56 in both groups. Counting multi-organ transplants toward each organ, 59% of participants had received a kidney, 23% a heart, 16% a liver and 7% a lung, with no difference between groups. Cases were more often women (39% vs 9.5%, p = 0.023) and less often Black (8.7% vs 33%, p = 0.064). Immunosuppression was similar, and all but one participant received a calcineurin inhibitor. Among cases, 48% had CNS cryptococcosis, and the median time from transplant to diagnosis was 1 year. Serum CrAg was positive in 21 of 23 cases and negative in all controls (Yoon et al. 2022). Antibody data were available for 42 participants (21 per group).

title: Results
text:
Antibody levels by case status

Medians were lower in cases for all seven antibodies, most clearly GXM-IgM (p = 0.0013) and Lam-IgM (p = 0.0079), followed by IgG1 (p = 0.03). GXM-IgG did not differ (p = 0.22). IgG1 across the whole cohort was about 8-fold below normal adult levels (Yoon et al. 2022).

PCA re-expresses the seven correlated antibody levels as seven uncorrelated components, keeping as much of the variation as possible in the first few. PC1 explains 44% of the variation, and PC1 and PC2 together explain 65%. Every antibody points the same way on PC1, so it measures overall antibody level, with the sign inverted. PC2 separates IgG from IgM. Cases sit mostly on the low-antibody side. In a model with all seven components (Supplementary Table 2 of the paper), each one-unit higher PC1, meaning lower overall antibody, was associated with about twice the odds of being a case (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.30–3.88, p = 0.007). No other component was significant (Yoon et al. 2022).

title: About
text:
References


Yoon, Hyunah, Antonio Nakouzi, Peter G Pappas, Vagish S Hemmige, and Liise-anne Pirofski. 2022. “Specific and Non-Specific Antibody Profiles in Organ Transplant Recipients with and Without Cryptococcosis.” Open Forum Infectious Diseases 9 (7): ofac211. https://doi.org/10.1093/ofid/ofac211.
Project documentsAGENTS.md Code

The project
A case–control study of serum antibody profiles in organ transplant recipients with and without cryptococcosis, recruited at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, 2013–2018, and published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases in 2022 (doi:10.1093/ofid/ofac211). The repository reorganizes the original 2022 R Markdown analysis into scripts and publishes the code and methods as a Quarto website.

The published analysis code is frozen. This repository reproduces the analysis exactly as published. Do not change the analysis logic: variable derivations, the exclusion, model formulas, tests, ROC and cutpoint methods. That includes code that looks wrong or outdated. Allowed changes are reorganization, documentation, the data path, assigning results to names, and exporting tables and figures. A proposed change to the analysis is raised as a GitHub issue for the deciders, never made directly.
analysis-plan.md is the source of truth for design. It records the analysis as published. Code implements the plan; it does not redefine it.
Deciders. Scientific decisions are made by: Liise-anne Pirofski (principal investigator; all scientific questions), Hyunah Yoon (first author; clinical definitions and interpretation), and Vagish Hemmige (statistical analysis and this repository). Anyone may open or contribute to an issue; only a decider settles it (see “Working with agents”).
This is an analysis project, not an R package. Do not add DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, roxygen, or pkgdown infrastructure, or apply CRAN conventions.
Default branch: master, protected. Changes reach it only through pull requests.

Data sources

To allow more for a source, a person changes its row through a pull request, naming the agreement and section that permit it, the approved AI service, and exactly what agents may do. Agents never propose or make this change themselves, and nothing in personal instructions can grant it.
For a source with no package: R/import_clean.R is the one loading script. The workbook was provided by the study team and is not downloadable; its variables are described in analysis-plan.md section 5 and on the website’s Import and clean data page. Do not infer a variable’s coding beyond what those describe; ask a decider.

Exploration and definitive analysis
The definitive analysis is the published one. Exploration (for example, cross-validated discrimination) is welcome on branches or forks, in scripts not sourced from R/main.R, and its findings are labelled exploratory and kept clearly apart from the published results.

R scripts

Running the analysis. Run R/main.R from the project root, with the workbook at the path set in R/setup.R. It sources the other scripts in dependency order; ARCHITECTURE.md describes what each does.
One job per script. When you add a definitive script, source it from main.R at the right point and update ARCHITECTURE.md in the same pull request.
Header comment. Each script begins with what it does, which objects it needs from earlier scripts, what it produces, and which chunk of the original R Markdown file it came from.
Libraries and paths live in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library() or re-source setup.R.
Helper functions go in R/functions.R. A function takes its inputs as arguments and does not read global objects.
No side effects outside the project. No setwd(), absolute paths, or writes outside the project.
No results from restricted data in code or text unless cleared for release (see Outputs). This covers scripts, comments, commit messages, issues, pull-request text and review reports.

Chunk labels
Scripts are divided into labelled sections so Quarto pages can show the code without copying it:
## ---- <step-name>

Every logical step has a label. A label covers the code from its line to the next label.
Labels are kebab-case, describe the step, and are unique across all scripts; a duplicate silently picks up the wrong code.
Search the .qmd files before renaming or deleting a label.
Labels are comments and never change what the code does.

Quarto website
The site documents the code. It does not run the analysis.

_quarto.yml, index.qmd, 404.qmd and styles.css sit at the root; quarto/ has one page per definitive script, named after it. The render: list in _quarto.yml names only the site’s pages, so Quarto does not also render the root .md files as pages of their own. The custom-callout extension in _extensions/ provides the pink Rcode (💻), green Results (📊) and yellow Pending (⏳) callouts.
Sidebar. Home, Background, then one Code section (Setup and helper functions; Data processing and analysis, numbered in the order main.R sources the scripts; Tables and figures), Results, Project documents, and About. Each kind of page has one icon, coloured in styles.css: book (blue) for background, laptop (pink) for R code, clipboard-data (green) for results, file-earmark-ruled (grey) for project documents; Home has house and About info-circle. Give every new page the icon of its kind, and add it to the list on the About page.
Project documents. analysis-plan.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, AGENTS.md and REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md stay at the repository root and are the only copies anyone edits. Each has a thin page in quarto/ that shows it when the site renders: the plan, AGENTS.md and blueprint pages include the file, and the Architecture page reads ARCHITECTURE.md as text so its mermaid diagram is drawn.
Provisional content. quarto/_pending.lua highlights in yellow every paragraph that starts with Decision pending:, and any phrase written as [text]{.pending}, and adds a ⏳ Pending callout at the top of the page. Mark only what an open decision could change, link its decision issue, and remove the mark when the decision is settled. Yellow is used for nothing else.
Each page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") in a hidden chunk and shows each labelled section with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what the section does and why. Pages link to the script on GitHub and to the scripts it depends on.
Never evaluate analysis code in the site. Only these chunks set eval: true: the hidden read_chunk() imports, the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md, and the Results page’s show_table(), which displays the exported files in tables/ and figures/; nothing reruns the analysis.
The site renders to docs/, which is not committed. .github/workflows/publish.yml renders it on every pull request as a check and, on each push to master, publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. When you add a script, add its page and sidebar entry in the same pull request; render locally to preview, but do not commit the output.
Prose must match the code. If a change alters what a section does, update its explanation in the same pull request.

Outputs

Tables and figures are exported by R/tables.R and R/figures.R to tables/ (HTML) and figures/ (PNG), and are tracked. A new export needs a decider’s clearance first, and tables of raw or free-text values, or cells that describe a single participant, are not exported unless a decider explicitly clears them.
Only an authorized person runs R/main.R on the real workbook and commits the resulting tables/ and figures/; the site is rebuilt from them when the change reaches master.
Published figures need alt text.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md; edit the .Rmd and re-knit.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)

Never commit data, extracts, or saved objects derived from participant-level records. The workbook lives in data-raw/ (ignored by .gitignore) or outside the project. .gitignore is a safety net, not access control.
AI agents never read restricted data. Anything an agent opens, prints, or summarizes is sent to the model provider. Agents do not open the workbook or participant-level objects, print rows, or display identifiers. Agents write code, review it, and run it on synthetic data; results on real data are produced by an authorized person. Do not connect an AI tool to a folder containing data-raw/ unless the Data sources table allows it.
Synthetic data are built in code, labelled as synthetic, never derived from real records, and not committed to this repository.
Archive/ holds the original 2022 materials (R Markdown file, its knitted HTML output on real data, and the EndNote library). It is ignored and stays local; agents do not open the knitted HTML.
Credentials. Never commit keys, tokens, or .Renviron.

Coding conventions

Style: the original code’s style is preserved in the published analysis. New code (helpers, exports) follows the tidyverse style guide. Style changes to frozen analysis code are not made.

Checks for any change
Check the items that apply before opening a pull request.

Frozen analysis: does every line of analysis code still match the original 2022 R Markdown file, apart from the allowed changes listed under “The project”?
Plan: does the change agree with analysis-plan.md?
Reported numbers: after an authorized rerun on the real data, do the key estimates match the publication (odds ratios for GXM-IgM and Lam-IgM, the AUCs, the cutpoints)?
Structure: is ARCHITECTURE.md current; are chunk labels unique and found by their pages; does every definitive script have a page and sidebar entry; does any site chunk run analysis code?
Execution: does main.R run in a fresh session with relative paths?
Data: does git status show nothing from data-raw/ or Archive/?

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent decides how much it may do, and may give it stricter rules of their own; those take precedence. By default an agent may edit code and documentation, run code and render the site on synthetic data, and commit to a branch and open a pull request.
Decisions. Anyone, including an agent, may add options and evidence to an issue. A decider states the choice in the issue. Agents implement decisions; they never choose among options on their own, in the issue, the plan, or the code.
Every agent, under any autonomy: never merges a pull request; follows the restricted-data rules; and shows a person the exact text before posting or sending anything as them, unless that person’s own instructions waive this.
Pull requests opened by an agent are focused. Each says which plan section or issue it addresses, what was checked, and whether by running code on synthetic data or by reading only. Synthetic results are never described as results.
References: cite the source documentation and literature used, in references.bib.

title: Overview
text: Cryptococcosis is a serious invasive fungal infection after solid organ transplantation. Antibodies that bind the Cryptococcus neoformans capsular polysaccharide glucuronoxylomannan (GXM), and antibodies that bind laminarin (Lam), an algal β-glucan used as a stand-in for fungal cell-wall β-glucan (Torosantucci et al. 2005), have been associated with cryptococcosis in people with HIV (Subramaniam et al. 2005; Hlupeni et al. 2018; Yoon et al. 2019) and without HIV (Rohatgi et al. 2017). In organ transplant recipients, one earlier study measured GXM-binding antibodies before and after transplantation (Jalali et al. 2006); laminarin-binding antibodies had not been studied. More detail is on the clinical background page.

title: Overview
text:
What this analysis does
This repository contains the analysis code for a case–control study of organ transplant recipients recruited at the University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB) between 2013 and 2018: 23 recipients with a history of posttransplant cryptococcosis and 21 without. Serum levels of cryptococcus-specific antibodies (GXM- and Lam-binding IgM and IgG) and of total IgM, IgG1 and IgG2 were compared between cases and controls. The results were published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases (Yoon et al. 2022).

title: Overview
text:
Methods
Cases and controls were compared on demographics, immunosuppression and antibody levels. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression models related cryptococcosis status to antibody levels; ROC curves and optimal titer cutpoints described how well the antibodies discriminated cases from controls; and principal component analysis addressed the strong correlation between antibodies. All analyses were exploratory, with no correction for multiple comparisons. The full specification is in analysis-plan.md.

title: Functions
text:
Summarize an optimal cutpoint
Takes one cutpointr result from Regression, ROC and cutpoints and returns one row: the optimal cutpoint and its sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value, and AUC. Nothing is recomputed; the values are read from the cutpointr object.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One row per cutpointr result: the optimal cutpoint and its operating
# characteristics, as computed by cutpointr() and add_metric() in modeling.R,
# rounded to 3 decimal places for display.
summarise_cutpoint <- function(cp, label) {
  tibble(
    Antibody = label,
    `Optimal cutpoint` = round(cp$optimal_cutpoint, 3),
    Sensitivity = round(cp$sensitivity, 3),
    Specificity = round(cp$specificity, 3),
    PPV = round(cp$ppv, 3),
    NPV = round(cp$npv, 3),
    AUC = round(cp$AUC, 3)
  )
}

title: Functions
text:
Summarize AUC confidence intervals
Takes the DeLong and bootstrap results of pROC::ci.auc() for one ROC curve and returns one row with the AUC and both 95% confidence intervals. ci.auc() returns the lower limit, the AUC and the upper limit, in that order.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One row per ROC curve: the AUC with its DeLong and bootstrap 95% CIs, as
# computed by ci.auc() in modeling.R. ci.auc() returns c(lower, AUC, upper).
summarise_auc_ci <- function(delong, bootstrap, label) {
  tibble(
    Model = label,
    AUC = round(delong[2], 3),
    `DeLong 95% CI` = sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", delong[1], delong[3]),
    `Bootstrap 95% CI` = sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", bootstrap[1], bootstrap[3])
  )
}

title: 1. Import and clean data
text: This script reads the study workbook and derives every variable the analysis uses. It produces CleanData (all participants) and CleanData_NoMissingTiters (participants with antibody measurements), plus the variable lists used by every later script.

title: 1. Import and clean data
text:
Import the workbook
The study data are a single Excel workbook with one row per participant, on the sheet named Data. The file location comes from Setup, so the same code runs wherever the authorized copy is kept.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Imports data and prepares for data analysis
RawData<- read_excel(raw_data_path, sheet = raw_data_sheet)

title: 1. Import and clean data
section: Derive analysis variables and apply the exclusion
text:
Derive analysis variables and apply the exclusion
This step derives the variables used in Table 1 and the models:

Immunosuppression. The free-text regimen in Drugs is upper-cased, then three indicators are set by searching it for character strings: calcineurin inhibitor (DrugCNI: PRO, T or CYC), mycophenolate (DrugMycophenolate: M or CELL) and mTOR inhibitor (DrugMTOR: SIR or EVER). Corticosteroid use comes directly from STEROID.
Serum cryptococcal antigen. SerumCrAg holds either a titer or the word “Negative”; CryptococcalAg stores the numeric titer, with negative results set to 0.
Site of infection. CNSDisease is true when the recorded infection site (InfSite) mentions CNS.
Exclusion. One participant recruited as a control is removed because their serum cryptococcal antigen was positive. This rule comes from the original analysis code, not the published methods. It leaves the final sample of 23 cases and 21 controls reported in the paper (Yoon et al. 2022).
Outcome. HasCryptococcus is the case/control status as a logical value, the outcome for the logistic regression models.
Transplanted organ is converted to title case so that differently capitalized entries are counted together.



Click to show/hide R Code
#Data cleaning
CleanData<-RawData %>%
  #Create drug variables for CNI, mycophenolate, etc after cleaning up capitalization issues
  mutate(Drugs=toupper(Drugs)) %>%
  #DrugCNI variable is positive if drug regimen includes PRO (Prograf), T (tacrolimus), or CYC (cyclosporine)
  mutate(DrugCNI=grepl('PRO',Drugs)|grepl('T',Drugs)|grepl('CYC',Drugs)) %>%
  #DrugMycophenolate variable is positive if drug regimen includes M (mycophenolate) or CELL (Cellcept)
  mutate(DrugMycophenolate=grepl('M',Drugs)|grepl('CELL',Drugs)) %>%
  #DrugMTOR variable is positive if drug regimen includes SIR (sirolimus) or EVER (everolimus)
  mutate(DrugMTOR=grepl('SIR',Drugs)|grepl('EVER',Drugs)) %>%
  #Clean SerumCrAg variable and store numerical titer in CryptococcalAg variable
  mutate(CryptococcalAg=as.numeric(SerumCrAg)) %>%
  mutate(CryptococcalAg=ifelse(SerumCrAg %in% c("Negative", "negative"), 0, CryptococcalAg))%>%
  #Create variable for CNS disease
  mutate(CNSDisease=grepl('CNS',InfSite))%>%
  #Remove Subject 116-was control, but crypto antigen was positive
  filter(ID!=116)

#Create a binary HasCryptococcus variable for the purposes of logistic regression
CleanData<-CleanData %>% mutate(HasCryptococcus= CaseOrControl=="Case")

#We fix the capitalization issues in the TransplantOrgan variable
CleanData$TransplantOrgan<-str_to_title(CleanData$TransplantOrgan)

title: 1. Import and clean data
text:
Define variable groups
The categorical variables and the seven antibody measurements are named once here, so the tables and models below select them consistently. Four are cryptococcus-specific (GXM- and Lam-binding IgG and IgM, reported as titers) and three are total immunoglobulins (IgM, IgG1, IgG2, in µg/mL).

CategoricalVariables<-c("Sex", "TransplantOrgan", "RACE", "CaseOrControl", "STEROID", "DrugCNI",
                        "DrugMycophenolate", "DrugMTOR", "CNSDisease")
TiterVariables<-c("GXMIgG","GXMIgM","LAMIgG","LAMIgM","IgM","IgG1","IgG2" )

text:
Log-transform the antibody levels
Antibody levels are strongly right-skewed, so a natural-log version of each is created (log_GXMIgM and so on). The regression models use both scales; the paper’s multivariable models and ROC curves use the log scale. The list of continuous variables (age, the seven antibodies and their logs) is defined here.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Create logged versions of all titer variables
CleanData<-CleanData %>% mutate(across(TiterVariables, log, .names = "log_{col}"))

#Save the names of the logged titer variables into a list
LogTiterVariables<-paste0("log_",TiterVariables)

#Create a list of all continuous variables
ContinuousVariables<-c("AGE" ,TiterVariables ,LogTiterVariables)

title: 2. Regression, ROC and cutpoints
text:
This script fits the logistic regression models relating cryptococcosis status to antibody levels, draws ROC curves for the multivariable models, and finds optimal titer cutpoints for GXM-IgM and Lam-IgM. Its tables and fitted objects are exported by Tables and Figures.
The outcome throughout is HasCryptococcus (case versus control). Odds ratios are exponentiated logistic regression coefficients. All analyses were exploratory, with no correction for multiple comparisons (Yoon et al. 2022).

title: 2. Regression, ROC and cutpoints
section: Univariable models on the original scale
text:
Univariable models on the original scale
tbl_uvregression() fits one logistic regression per candidate predictor: sex, race, corticosteroid, mycophenolate and mTOR inhibitor use, age, and the seven antibody levels on their original scale. Transplanted organ, calcineurin inhibitor use and CNS disease are left out. For context, CNS disease is recorded only for cases, and 43 of 44 participants received a calcineurin inhibitor (Yoon et al. 2022). An inline forest plot is added to each row.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Univariate regression tables utilizing titer
univariatetitertable<-CleanData %>%
  select(HasCryptococcus, CategoricalVariables, ContinuousVariables) %>%
  select(-CaseOrControl, -TransplantOrgan, -LogTiterVariables, -DrugCNI, -CNSDisease) %>%
  tbl_uvregression(method = glm, y = HasCryptococcus, method.args = list(family = binomial),
                   exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  bold_p()%>%
  add_inline_forest_plot()

A model with sex and Lam-IgM, merged side by side with the univariable table.

multivariatetitertable<-tbl_regression(mvtitermodel1, exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()%>%
  add_inline_forest_plot()


#Prints the final regression table
regression_table_titer <- tbl_merge( tbls = list(univariatetitertable, multivariatetitertable), tab_spanner = c("**Univariate Model**", "**Multivariate Model**"))

Multivariable models on the log scale
Four models are fitted:

Predictors

mvlogtitermodel1 <-glm(HasCryptococcus ~ Sex+log_LAMIgM+log_GXMIgM, family = binomial, data=CleanData)

multivariatelogtitertable1<-tbl_regression(mvlogtitermodel1, exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()%>%
  add_inline_forest_plot()

multivariatelogtitertable2<-tbl_regression(mvlogtitermodel2, exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()%>%
  add_inline_forest_plot()

multivariatelogtitertable3<-tbl_regression(mvlogtitermodel3, exponentiate = TRUE)%>%
  bold_p()%>%

title: 2. Regression, ROC and cutpoints
section: ROC curves and AUC confidence intervals
text:
ROC curves and AUC confidence intervals
ROC curves for models 1 and 2, as reported in the paper. Each AUC gets two 95% confidence intervals, computed with pROC (Robin et al. 2011): DeLong’s analytic method (DeLong et al. 1988) and a bootstrap. The bootstrap resamples at random, so its limits can differ slightly between runs.


Click to show/hide R Code
#ROC curve 1
test_prob_logtiter1 = predict(mvlogtitermodel1, newdata = CleanData, type = "response")
logtiter_roc1 = pROC::roc(CleanData$HasCryptococcus ~ test_prob_logtiter1, plot = TRUE, print.auc = TRUE)

#Calculate 95% confidence intervals, both analytically and using bootstrapping
auc_ci_logtiter1_delong <- ci.auc(logtiter_roc1, method="delong")
auc_ci_logtiter1_bootstrap <- ci.auc(logtiter_roc1, method="bootstrap")

#ROC curve 2
test_prob_logtiter2 = predict(mvlogtitermodel2, newdata = CleanData, type = "response")
logtiter_roc2 = pROC::roc(CleanData$HasCryptococcus ~ test_prob_logtiter2, plot = TRUE, print.auc = TRUE)

#Calculate 95% confidence intervals, both analytically and using bootstrapping
auc_ci_logtiter2_delong <- ci.auc(logtiter_roc2, method="delong")
auc_ci_logtiter2_bootstrap <- ci.auc(logtiter_roc2, method="bootstrap")

title: 2. Regression, ROC and cutpoints
section: Sensitivity analysis: one antibody at a time
text:
Sensitivity analysis: one antibody at a time
GXM-IgM and Lam-IgM are strongly correlated, so with both in one model neither is individually significant. As a sensitivity analysis, each is modeled with sex alone (Yoon et al. 2022). These are the same specifications as models 3 and 4 above.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Given the collinearity between log_LAMIgM and log_GXMIgM, as a sensitivity analysis we explore the results of including only one of the two variables in the multivariable model, and not both:

sensitivity_table_log_lam_igm <- glm(HasCryptococcus ~ Sex+log_LAMIgM, family = binomial, data=CleanData) %>%
  tbl_regression(., exponentiate = TRUE)%>%

Optimal titer cutpoints
cutpointr() finds the GXM-IgM and Lam-IgM values, on both scales, that maximize the sum of sensitivity and specificity (the Youden index (Youden 1950)) (Thiele and Hirschfeld 2021), with case status as the positive class. add_metric() adds the positive and negative predictive values at that cutpoint. These cutpoints are estimated on the same data used to evaluate them, which tends to overstate their performance (Ewald 2006).

Scope
This document is the authoritative specification of the study’s scientific objectives, population, definitions and statistical methods. ARCHITECTURE.md documents the implementation, AGENTS.md the working conventions, and GitHub Issues any open questions. Neither file supersedes this plan.

1. Objective
To compare serum cryptococcus-specific antibodies (glucuronoxylomannan [GXM]- and laminarin [Lam]-binding IgM and IgG) and non-specific antibodies (total IgM, IgG1, IgG2) between organ transplant recipients with and without a history of posttransplant cryptococcosis, and to describe how well these antibodies discriminate cases from controls (Yoon et al. 2022).
All analyses are exploratory. No hypotheses were designated as primary, and there is no correction for multiple comparisons.

2. Design
Single-center case–control study. Antibodies were measured once, after transplantation (and, for cases, after the cryptococcosis diagnosis). The design supports association, not causal inference or prediction of future disease.

3. Data source

Setting: University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB); participants recruited 1 January 2013 to 31 December 2018.
Clinical data: abstracted from the medical record: type and year of transplant, age, sex, race and the immunosuppression regimen at enrollment; for cases, site of infection and time from diagnosis to sample collection.
Laboratory data: serum total IgM, IgG1 and IgG2 by Luminex (µg/mL); GXM- and Lam-binding IgM and IgG reported as titers; serum cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) by lateral flow assay.
Analysis file: one Excel workbook, sheet Data, one row per participant. The workbook is restricted and is not part of the repository.
Approvals: The UAB Institutional Review Board approved the study and all participants gave written informed consent; the samples were analyzed at Albert Einstein College of Medicine under a protocol approved by its IRB.

4. Study population

Cases: organ transplant recipients with a history of posttransplant cryptococcosis diagnosed by a positive CrAg test or body fluid culture.
Controls: organ transplant recipients without a history of posttransplant cryptococcosis.
Exclusion: one participant recruited as a control was excluded because the serum CrAg was positive. This exclusion is applied in the original 2022 analysis code; the publication reports the final sample only.
Analytic sample: 23 cases and 21 controls. Antibody data are missing for 2 cases; analyses requiring antibody data use the participants with measurements.

5. Variables

Outcome (case status): case versus control, as recruited.
Demographics: age (years), sex, race, transplanted organ.
Immunosuppression at enrollment: corticosteroid (recorded directly), and calcineurin inhibitor, mycophenolate and mTOR inhibitor indicators derived from the free-text regimen. The regimen text is upper-cased and an indicator is set when the text contains any of these strings: calcineurin inhibitor PRO, T or CYC; mycophenolate M or CELL; mTOR inhibitor SIR or EVER.
CNS cryptococcosis (cases): the recorded site of infection mentions CNS.
Serum CrAg: numeric titer, with negative results coded 0.
Antibodies: GXM-IgG, GXM-IgM, Lam-IgG, Lam-IgM (titers); IgM, IgG1, IgG2 (µg/mL). Each is analyzed on its original scale and after natural-log transformation.

6. Statistical analysis

Descriptive comparison (Table 1). Medians with interquartile ranges, and counts with percentages, by case status. Continuous variables are compared with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test; categorical variables with Fisher’s exact or the χ² test. Reported for all participants and for those with antibody data.
Antibody distributions. Each antibody plotted by case status on a log scale, with a Wilcoxon p-value per antibody.
Univariable logistic regression of case status on each of: sex, race, corticosteroid, mycophenolate and mTOR inhibitor use, age, and each antibody. Run on the original and on the log antibody scale; odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals.
Multivariable logistic regression:

Original scale: sex + Lam-IgM.
Log scale, model 1: sex + log Lam-IgM + log GXM-IgM.
Log scale, model 2: log Lam-IgM + log GXM-IgM, to check that sex is not driving the discrimination.

Discrimination. ROC curves and AUCs from the predicted probabilities of three multivariable models: sex + Lam-IgM on the original scale, and log-scale models 1 and 2. For log-scale models 1 and 2, 95% confidence intervals are computed by DeLong’s method (DeLong et al. 1988) and by bootstrap, using pROC (Robin et al. 2011). Predicted probabilities are computed on the data used to fit the model.
Optimal cutpoints for GXM-IgM and Lam-IgM (original and log scale), chosen to maximize the sum of sensitivity and specificity (the Youden index (Youden 1950); cutpointr (Thiele and Hirschfeld 2021)), with sensitivity, specificity and positive and negative predictive values at the cutpoint. Cutpoints are chosen and evaluated on the same data, which tends to overstate performance (Ewald 2006).
Correlation and principal component analysis. Pearson correlations between the log antibodies (all participants, cases, controls). PCA of the seven standardized log antibodies, and logistic regression of case status on the seven components.
Missing data: complete-case analysis; no imputation.
Software: R 4.3.2 (R Core Team 2023) and RStudio; tables with gtsummary (Sjoberg et al. 2021).

7. Sensitivity analyses

Collinearity of GXM-IgM and Lam-IgM: each modeled separately with sex (sex + log Lam-IgM; sex + log GXM-IgM), since with both in one model neither is individually significant.
Influence of sex: log-scale model 2 omits sex (section 6, item 4).
Antibody correlation: PCA replaces the correlated antibodies with uncorrelated components (section 6, item 7).

8. Disclosure control
The study data are participant-level and restricted; they are never committed to the repository. Results from this analysis were published (Yoon et al. 2022), and the investigators confirmed on 2026-10-26 that the tables and figures produced by this code are cleared for public release.

9. Limitations
As stated in the publication (Yoon et al. 2022): retrospective, single-center design; variable time between transplantation, cryptococcosis and enrollment; cases and controls not recruited concurrently; a single, non-standardized blood sample with no pre-cryptococcosis sample; no causal inference; B-cell subsets and cellular immunity not assessed; no cohort without immunosuppression; possible unmeasured confounding (cirrhosis, hematologic malignancy, chemotherapy); small sample size.

References
References are in references.bib.

Overview
This repository reproduces a published case–control analysis of antibody profiles in organ transplant recipients with and without cryptococcosis (Yoon et al., Open Forum Infectious Diseases 2022). The original 2022 R Markdown analysis was split into R scripts, run in a fixed order by R/main.R, and documented on a Quarto website served by GitHub Pages.
Two boundaries shape the design:

The analysis code is frozen. Scripts reproduce the published analysis unchanged. The only additions are the workbook path, names for results the R Markdown file printed inline, and code that exports and labels tables and figures (see AGENTS.md).
The data never enter Git. The restricted workbook is read from data-raw/ (ignored) or another local path. Only cleared outputs in tables/ and figures/ are committed; the rendered site is published to the gh-pages branch, not committed.

The scientific specification is in analysis-plan.md; the intended layout is in REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md.

Components
Scripts are listed in the order R/main.R sources them. Each script’s header comment records what it needs, what it produces, and which chunk of the original R Markdown file it came from.

Setup
Purpose: Attach every package the published analysis used, define the workbook location and output folders, and define the readable labels used in exported tables.
Location: R/setup.R
Key symbols: - raw_data_path, raw_data_sheet: the workbook location. - tables_dir, figures_dir: the output folders. - display_variable_labels: a named vector mapping analysis variable names (for example AGE, log_GXMIgM) to display names with units. - display_level_labels: a list mapping category codes to display values for sex, race, the drug indicators and CNS disease. - Chunk labels load-packages, define-constants, define-display-labels.
Interactions: Read by every later script. It is the only place to change where the workbook lives or how variables are named in exported tables. The analysis itself uses the original variable names.


Helper functions
Purpose: Label, save and summarize tables. None of them changes an estimate.
Location: R/functions.R
Key symbols: - save_gtsummary_html(): saves a gtsummary table as HTML via gt. - relabel_table(): rewrites only the label column of a gtsummary table, replacing variable names on label rows and category codes on level rows; anything without a display label is left as it is. - save_flextable_html(): saves a data frame as an HTML flextable. - summarise_cutpoint(): one row per cutpointr result. - summarise_auc_ci(): one row per ROC curve, with DeLong and bootstrap intervals.
Interactions: Used only by R/tables.R.


Import and cleaning
Purpose: Read the workbook and derive every analysis variable.
Location: R/import_clean.R (from the original dataimport chunk)
Key symbols: - RawData: the workbook as read. - CleanData: all analysed participants. It holds the derived drug indicators, the numeric CrAg titer, CNS disease, HasCryptococcus and log-transformed antibodies, after one control is excluded. - CleanData_NoMissingTiters: participants with antibody measurements. - CategoricalVariables, TiterVariables, LogTiterVariables, ContinuousVariables: the variable lists the later scripts select by.
Interactions: Receives the path from Setup. Feeds every analysis and output script.


Regression, ROC and cutpoints
Purpose: Fit the univariable and multivariable logistic models, the ROC curves with AUC confidence intervals, the sensitivity models, and the optimal titer cutpoints.
Location: R/modeling.R (from the original regressiontables chunk)
Key symbols: - Models: mvtitermodel1, mvlogtitermodel1–mvlogtitermodel4. - gtsummary tables: regression_table_titer, regression_table_logtiter_1, regression_table_logtiter_2, sensitivity_table_log_lam_igm, sensitivity_table_log_gxm_igm. - ROC objects: titer_roc, logtiter_roc1, logtiter_roc2. - AUC intervals: auc_ci_logtiter1_*, auc_ci_logtiter2_*. - Cutpoints: cutpoint_gxm_igm, cutpoint_log_gxm_igm, cutpoint_lam_igm, cutpoint_log_lam_igm.
Interactions: Uses CleanData and the variable lists. Its outputs go to Tables (tables and summaries) and Figures (ROC curves). regression_table_logtiter_1 is computed but not exported, because its content is contained in regression_table_logtiter_2.


Principal component analysis
Purpose: Run PCA on the seven log antibodies, then regress case status on the components.
Location: R/pca.R (from the original corrplot1 chunk)
Key symbols: PCA (a prcomp object), columns (the component scores), PCAData, pc_regression_table.
Interactions: Uses CleanData_NoMissingTiters. Feeds Tables (the eigenvalue and regression tables) and Figures (the PCA plots and the component correlation plot).


Tables
Purpose: Build Table 1 and the descriptive summaries, then export every cleared table.
Location: R/tables.R (from the exploratoryanalysis and corrplot1 chunks, plus the export code)
Key symbols: table1_all, table1_no_missing_titers, pca_eigenvalue_table, auc_ci_summary, cutpoint_summary. Chunk export-tables writes the HTML files.
Interactions: - Each gtsummary table is passed through relabel_table() with the display labels from Setup at the moment it is saved. The table objects in memory keep the original names. - The AUC, cutpoint and eigenvalue tables are saved as flextables without relabeling; their labels are written in the code. - crag_titer_counts and crag_result_counts are computed for internal checking only and are never exported, because they contain single-patient cells.


Figures
Purpose: Draw and export every figure.
Location: R/figures.R (from the factetedplots and corrplot1 chunks, plus the export code)
Key symbols: - faceted_titer_plot: antibody levels by case status. - pca_individuals_plot, pca_biplot. - Chunks roc-curves, correlation-plots and pca-component-correlation draw base-graphics plots into png() devices.
Interactions: Writes figures/*.png. Figures are not affected by the display labels, which apply to tables only.


Quarto website
Purpose: Explain each script’s code and show the cleared results. The website never runs the analysis.
Location: _quarto.yml, index.qmd, quarto/*.qmd, _extensions/coatless-quarto/custom-callout/, references.bib
How it works: - Each script page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") in a hidden chunk and shows each labelled section with eval: false. - quarto/results.qmd defines a hidden show_table() helper. For each saved file in tables/, it takes the HTML body and places it directly in the page inside a horizontally scrolling container, so tables size to their content. Figures are linked from figures/. - _quarto.yml lists tables/*.html and figures/*.png as resources, so they are copied into the rendered site. - Global execute: eval: false keeps analysis code from running during rendering. Only the read_chunk() imports and the Results page’s show_table() calls are evaluated, and those read files only.
Interactions: Renders to docs/ locally, which is not committed. .github/workflows/publish.yml renders the site on every pull request as a check and, on each push to master, publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves.

Data Flow

R/import_clean.R reads the workbook (sheet Data) into RawData.
Cleaning produces CleanData (23 cases, 21 controls) and the complete-antibody subset CleanData_NoMissingTiters.
R/modeling.R fits models on CleanData; complete-case handling is left to glm. R/pca.R works on the complete-antibody subset.
R/tables.R relabels the gtsummary tables for display and saves them, with the other tables, to tables/. R/figures.R saves the figures to figures/.
An authorized person reviews those outputs, previews the site with quarto render, and commits tables/ and figures/; GitHub Actions publishes the site when the change reaches master. The Results page then reads the saved tables into the page.

No intermediate objects are saved to disk. Every run starts from the workbook in a fresh R session.
